Maria Claudia, this is Greg Novak in Pittsburgh. I am sorry to do this on a voicemail, but I promised you a heads-up the moment I knew anything, so here it is. The May container did not sail on Tuesday. It is still at the port, and the reason is a customs hold on a different shipment that was loaded in front of ours. Nobody has done anything wrong, and nothing is damaged. What I can tell you is this. The line is loading again on Thursday, and our freight desk says the vessel departs on the tenth. I am not going to promise you an arrival date in Brazil, because I do not know it yet, and I would rather tell you that I do not know than give you a date that moves again next week. Two things I would ask. First, please do not let anyone tell your board that this is a production problem, because it is not. The goods were finished on time. Second, if the tenth does not work for you, call me today and I will tell you exactly what the other options cost. I will send the written version of all of this before six o'clock.

I have passed on thousands of messages in thirty years, and the one I still think about is four words long. A supplier called me on a Friday and said, we can hold the price, but only if the volume holds. When I passed it on to my team, I said he had agreed to hold the price. I dropped the condition, because the call had been friendly and I did not want to end the week on a bad note. I downplayed it, and I told myself I was being positive. Three weeks later the volume fell, the price went up exactly as he had said it would, and I had to explain to my own board why I had told them something that was never true. He had not misled me. I had misquoted him, by leaving out the half that mattered. Since then I do two things. When a condition is attached, I write the sentence down verbatim and I read it back to the person on the call. And when I relay it, I say who said it and I say the whole thing, even when the whole thing is uncomfortable. A message that arrives smaller than it left is not good news. It is a bill that arrives later.

First, while the other side is still speaking, you write the condition down in their own words, so that nothing has to be rebuilt from memory afterwards. Then, before the call ends, you read that line back to them and you ask them to clarify anything you are not sure about. After that, you decide what belongs in the readout and what does not, and you flag the one line that changes a decision. Next, you relay it with the name of the person who said it, and you keep the part that is uncomfortable, because a message that arrives smaller than it left is a bill that arrives later. Finally, you send the written version the same day, and you say clearly which parts are verbatim and which parts are your own summary.
